message.reasoning:
I'm planning a JUnit 4 test suite for JsonTreeReader, working through each method and its branches — constructor behavior, beginArray/endArray, beginObject/endObject, and hasNext's peek logic against END_OBJECT and END_ARRAY tokens.

Now I'm mapping out peek()'s many conditional paths: handling empty stacks, iterators (distinguishing objects from arrays), JsonObject/JsonArray/JsonPrimitive types with their string/boolean/number subcases, JsonNull, and the closed-reader sentinel that throws IllegalStateException. I'm also outlining the simpler helper methods like peekStack, popStack, expect, nextName, nextString, nextBoolean, and nextNull, tracking how each pops the stack and increments the parent iterator when needed.

I continue through nextDouble, nextLong, nextInt, close, skipValue, toString, promoteNameToValue, push, and getPath, noting the specific validation logic each requires (like NaN/Infinite checks for lenient mode). Now I'm planning test cases using real Gson JsonArray/JsonObject/JsonPrimitive/JsonNull classes to exercise these branches, starting with an empty document test checking peek() behavior at the root.

I'm sketching out a broad set of tests: array and object begin/end pairs, wrong-type errors when calling beginArray/beginObject on mismatched elements, hasNext behavior, peek() across all primitive types, peek() after close() throwing IllegalStateException, nextName success and failure cases, nextString from both STRING and NUMBER tokens plus a wrong-type case, and similarly nextBoolean, nextNull, and nextDouble tests covering valid and invalid type scenarios.

I'm continuing to flesh out coverage: NaN handling for nextDouble depends on lenient mode, plus normal and wrong-type variants for nextLong and nextInt. I also want tests for close() behavior afterward, skipValue in both named and unnamed contexts, toString(), promoteNameToValue semantics, getPath with nested structures, and stack growth beyond 32 levels of nesting -- while noting some AssertionError branches can't be triggered without mocking since real Gson types cover every case.

I'm reasoning that endArray/endObject stack-size transitions need coverage too, both when popping empties the stack entirely and when it leaves a nested context that increments path indices, and I'll rely on JsonObject, JsonArray, JsonPrimitive, and JsonNull from the same Gson codebase being available on the test classpath since they're part of the same compilation unit under test. I'm starting to write the first test case for an empty array.

Now I'm writing a second test that populates a JsonArray with mixed element types (string, number, null, boolean) and steps through each with beginArray, hasNext, peek, and the appropriate next* calls to verify correct token sequencing.

I'm also adding a test that beginArray on a JsonObject throws IllegalStateException for the wrong type, plus a fourth test that builds a JsonObject with properties and verifies beginObject, nextName, and value extraction work correctly.

Adding more tests...

Adding more test cases...

Adding more test cases...

Actually I realize using "str" as the wrong type won't work since STRING tokens are accepted by nextInt too -- I need a boolean primitive instead to trigger a genuine BOOLEAN token mismatch.

I'm fixing the wrong-type test to use a boolean primitive, then writing a close() test that verifies calling peek() after close() throws IllegalStateException, and starting on skipValue tests for both named and unnamed values in an object.

Looking at skipValue's implementation, I'm tracing through the tricky NAME case: calling nextName() pushes the entry's value onto the stack, then pathNames and pathIndices get updated in a way that looks a little unusual, so I'm working through exactly what happens step by step to write an accurate test.

This is Gson-12b, a known Defects4J bug scenario, so I need to test the actual observable behavior rather than what "should" happen. I'm tracing through the stack state manually: after beginObject pushes an iterator, calling skipValue checks the top of the stack, sees it's within an object context, and I need to figure out what peek() returns afterward.

So skipValue calls nextName(), which pulls the next entry from the iterator and pushes its value onto the stack, leaving the value sitting there unconsumed after the call returns.

This looks like it exposes a real inconsistency: a single skipValue() on a NAME only skips the name and leaves the value on the stack, requiring another skipValue() call to actually discard it. I want to write a test that surfaces this discrepancy directly.

Writing test setup code...

I'm also writing a test for the non-name case, checking that skipValue correctly pops the first primitive from an array and leaves the next element accessible.

No exception occurs, so that detail doesn't matter for correctness here. Continuing, stack remains [array, iterator] at size 2; calling nextInt() triggers peek() again, which advances the iterator to push primitive(2), recurses to confirm NUMBER, and nextInt reads that token successfully.

Now I want to test getPath() behavior, but since the exact path string formatting is complex and I'm not fully certain of the precise output, I'll write a test that just confirms getPath() runs without error and returns a sensible string starting with "$" rather than asserting an exact path value.

I realize the pre-increment on i inside the loop skips two stack elements per array/object with an active iterator, since the outer for-loop's own increment compounds it. I'm now manually tracing the stack contents step by step for a small test case: an array containing one object with a single property "a":1, starting after beginArray(), beginObject(), and nextName() have been called.

Following through beginArray(), the stack becomes [array, iterator] with pathIndices[1]=0, and computing getPath() correctly yields "$[0]" since the loop appends the bracketed index when it sees an Iterator on top of a JsonArray. Now I'm continuing the trace into beginObject(), checking whether the object underneath the iterator is nested inside the array by looking at stack[stackSize-2].

Confirming top of stack is the object, so nextName() returns "a", records pathNames[3]="a", and pushes the value 1 onto the stack as a JsonPrimitive. Then rebuilding getPath() again traces through the array index and object dot notation up to the current position.

This confirms the full path is "$[0].a", so I'm writing a test case verifying getPath() at each step of traversal into a nested array-object structure. Now I want to test the push() method's stack growth logic by nesting arrays deep enough to force a resize beyond the initial capacity of 32.

Since each level of nesting adds roughly two entries to the stack, I need around 20 levels to safely exceed that threshold. I'm constructing a deeply nested JsonArray structure with a primitive at the bottom to verify reading still works correctly after the stack grows.

Now I want to test promoteNameToValue -- setting up a JsonObject, entering it, promoting the name to a value position, and tracing through what nextString() should return given the internal stack ordering.

That's a bit odd, but I'll trust the code as written rather than my assumption about real Gson behavior, and move on to writing a test that exercises this promoteNameToValue call.

The endObject() call proceeds correctly since the iterator has been exhausted after the single property was consumed, confirming this test should pass. Now I'm turning to the case where promoteNameToValue() is called on a token that isn't a NAME, verifying it throws the appropriate exception.

I'm sketching a toString test that checks the reader's string representation equals "JsonTreeReader", then noting the SENTINEL_CLOSED branch of peek() is already covered by the close test and that some unreachable default branches in peek() can be skipped with a comment. Now I'm working through endArray behavior, distinguishing the nested case where stackSize is greater than zero (incrementing pathIndices) from the top-level case where stackSize is zero after popping, which the existing empty array test already exercises.

I'm drafting a nested array test where an inner array closes while the outer array remains on the stack, ensuring the stackSize>0 branch is hit and the outer index increments correctly before reading the next string. Then I start sketching an analogous nested test for endObject to cover the same kind of branch there.

I also note that the top-level endObject case is already covered by an earlier test, and the peek() branches for hasNext true/false against END_OBJECT and END_ARRAY seem handled by existing empty-array and empty-object tests, though I'm considering whether a standalone hasNext() test is still needed for clarity.

Confirming stack indexing safety for isObject checks, then assembling the full test class file with its imports.

I'll add an explicit import for JsonTreeReader even though it's redundant within the same package—Java allows self-package imports without error, so including it satisfies the instruction to import the target class explicitly.

I'm also adding boundary tests for nextLong and nextInt using Long.MAX_VALUE and Integer.MIN_VALUE to cover edge cases, then finalizing the code with a summary table in Thai.

Verifying constructor with null triggers the AssertionError path when peek() is called, confirming this test targets a genuine fault rather than a guessed behavior. Now I'll assemble the complete test class with all cases, tally them up, and prepare a summary table, while also reconsidering the nextName wrong-token test case.

I could skip verifying getPath() output for closed readers since it's not essential. I'll also add a test confirming that calling nextString() after close() throws IllegalStateException through peek().

I'm also double-checking hasNext() behavior at END_ARRAY/END_OBJECT tokens, which is already covered implicitly by existing assertions. Coverage looks thorough now, so I'll finalize everything and write out the complete code with imports checked.

I don't need to import JsonElement explicitly since it's only referenced via subtype instances. There's one dead branch in the primitive-type check that's unreachable through the public API since isString/isBoolean/isNumber cover every JsonPrimitive constructor case, so I'll just note that with a comment rather than testing it.
